draft.title: How useful a source is
card: No source is useful or useless on its own. How useful it is depends on the question a historian is asking.
Historians ask who made the source, when it was made, why it was made and who it was made for.
A source made to persuade or to praise may leave out facts. It can still be useful, for example to show what the maker wanted people to believe.
A source made close to an event may be well informed. A source made long after may know the outcome but can be less reliable on small details.
draft.remember: Usefulness depends on the maker, the time, the purpose, the audience and the question.

a.q: A student says a source is useless because it was written to persuade people. What is the best reply?
opts: It may still help answer a question about the maker's aims
It is useless, because any source with a purpose is false
It helps with every question, because it is old
It is useless unless it was made long after the event
a.why: A source's purpose affects what it can show, but it does not make it useless. A persuasive source can show the maker's aims and beliefs. The tempting wrong answer says purpose makes a source false, but a source with a purpose may leave things out rather than be false.
a.clue: Think about which question the source could help answer.

b.q: Priya is studying how a Victorian goldfield town was run in 1853. She finds a poster the town's police camp made to warn diggers to buy licences. Why is it useful for her question?
opts: It shows what rules the officials wanted diggers to follow
It gives a fair account of how diggers felt about the rules
It must be accurate, because officials made it
It is useful only because it is a primary source
b.why: The poster was made by officials for diggers, so it shows the rules they wanted enforced. It does not show what diggers felt, because diggers did not make it. The tempting wrong answer treats an official source as neutral, but who made it and why still matter.
b.clue: Ask who made the poster and who it was meant for.

a.best: It may still help answer a question about the maker's aims

b.best: It shows what rules the officials wanted diggers to follow

a.q: A student says a speech written to persuade voters is useless. Which reply best shows how a historian could use it?
opts: It can show what the speaker wanted voters to believe
It can show all the facts, as speeches leave nothing out
It can show how voters at the time felt about the speech
It can be used once its persuasive parts are cut out
a.why: A persuasive speech may leave out facts, but it can show the speaker's aims and what they wanted people to believe. The tempting wrong answer is about voters' feelings: the speaker made the speech, so it shows the speaker's view, not how voters reacted.
a.clue: Think about who made the speech and why.

b.q: Priya is studying how a Victorian goldfield town was run in 1853. She finds a poster the town's police camp made to warn diggers to buy licences. What can the poster show her?
opts: What rules the officials wanted diggers to follow
How diggers felt about the rules they had to obey
That the rules were obeyed, because officials made it
How often diggers broke the licence rules in 1853
b.why: The poster was made by officials for diggers, so it shows the rules officials wanted followed. It does not show what diggers felt, because diggers did not make it. A warning also cannot prove the rules were obeyed or how often they were broken.
b.clue: Ask who made the poster and who it was meant for.
